display_title: The Convergence of Trump and AI
short_summary: The Trump administration is deepening its ties with major AI firms, integrating the technology into military and intelligence operations.

image.credit: Fibonacci Blue from Minnesota, USA · CC BY 2.0

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Trump makes it clear his power is becoming entwined with AI

paragraphs: The landscape of American governance is undergoing a profound transformation as the Trump administration aligns its executive power with the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence. In a series of strategic maneuvers, the White House has fostered unprecedented alliances with Silicon Valley, effectively blurring the lines between private corporate interests and federal policy. Last week, President Trump convened with six prominent AI CEOs to sign what was described as a 'morally binding' agreement. This framework, which emphasizes self-regulation, was reportedly drafted by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, who circulated the draft before the meeting. While the President likened the document to a constitution, critics note that it lacks legal enforceability, raising questions about the influence of tech giants on the drafting of executive orders.

Beyond policy agreements, the administration has initiated a linguistic rebrand, mandating that all government documents refer to 'artificial intelligence' as 'super intelligence.' This shift has already seen adoption among key allies, such as Elon Musk, who renamed a SpaceX subsidiary to reflect the new terminology. Musk’s involvement in the administration has deepened further; Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recently appointed him to 'Project Meridian,' a taskforce alongside Palmer Luckey and Emil Michael. This group is dedicated to achieving absolute technological dominance in future warfare, with a report on their findings expected in 120 days. This initiative underscores the administration's intent to leverage private sector innovation for military and intelligence objectives.

Perhaps the most significant development is the appointment of Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, as the administration's AI czar. Unlike his predecessor, David Sacks—a venture capitalist who championed deregulation while maintaining financial stakes in AI firms—Clayton’s dual role suggests that the government views AI primarily as a tool for enhancing offensive capabilities, particularly in surveillance and intelligence gathering. This integration of spy agencies into AI policy carries significant global implications, as other nations may find their own technological sovereignty challenged by the US-led model.

Despite the intense focus on AI, economic data presents a more nuanced reality. While the stock market has been heavily buoyed by the growth of AI-related companies over the past five years, the broader labor market tells a different story. According to recent federal jobs reports, the majority of new hiring in the United States is occurring in the healthcare sector rather than the tech industry. This suggests that while AI may be a powerful engine for GDP growth and military strategy, it is not yet the primary driver of job creation on a national scale. As these alliances solidify, the administration faces the challenge of balancing the promise of automated power with the practical needs of the American workforce.

facts.fact: Donald Trump signed a non-binding AI agreement with six tech CEOs, including Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jensen Huang.
The White House has rebranded 'artificial intelligence' to 'super intelligence' in official government documents.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appointed Elon Musk to a taskforce called Project Meridian to study future warfare.
Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, has been appointed as the administration's AI czar.
Recent US jobs data indicates that AI is not the primary driver of national job creation, with healthcare sectors hiring more workers.
